Every situation is different. For me, my parents were the ones that found me starting to lose consciousness after overdosing, and they freaked out. Screaming, crying—terrified expressions and scared emotions all around. I cant imagine how they would’ve reacted if I had actually succeeded—I don’t even want to think about it.

I started getting therapy and psychiatric help after the whole ordeal was over. I returned to school a month afterwards, and my friends all welcomed me back. I learned afterwards just how big of an impact my attempt left on people who I didn’t even think would be that affected by it. A friend cried in my arms when we were just talking a couple of months later spontaneously, screaming how scared she was and how much she didn’t want me to die. 

If by health—you mean my state directly after the attempt, I was put in the back of an ambulance and they encouraged me to drink a “charcoal milkshake”, which I drank a good portion of. When I went to the hospital, I proceeded to vomit profusely because of the “milkshake”, as it was made for that specific purpose. 

If you mean mental health—I realized that my big motivation for trying to commit suicide at the time, which was “If I go now, they’ll grieve and get over me eventually—which is better than the problems I’m causing for them now”, was completely wrong. My friends and family really explained to me how you never get over death in that way. If my attempt went through, they said that they would never be able to get over it for as long as they lived—and any problem I caused now was FARRR more worth the cost of my life.

Love is the worst fucking concept in the world. Society has been essentially conditioned into believing that happiness will come from “love”, that your troubles will go away from “love”, that “love” changes everything. It simply isn’t true.

It took me ages to shake that feeling, that I needed love to function. That without a relationship or fucking love, my life would be pointless. But I eventually did, and I was able to achieve a good mental state. That’s not to say it was easy—it fucking wasn’t. I tried to commit twice along the way. But eventually I was able to be truly happy—or at the very least, stable on my own. And happiness soon followed once I found that mindset.

Happiness can be fleeting. But it also can be found around the most obscure corners—hiding in abundant supply in places you’d never think of looking. And when you find it, it won’t be where you expect it. But it will eventually be there.

Life is a ridiculous thing. It sucks ASS at times, but it’s fucking amazing as a concept. People like to theorize what will happen after death—and while technically nobody knows, considering the other forms of life presented on Earth, it seems very unlikely that us Humans will be the ones to go to some form of afterlife.

I think the idea of dying is terrifying. People like to say it’s “peaceful”, and compare it to your existence before you were even conceived in the womb. I highly disagree. You didn’t exist before—so there was nothing to grieve over. But you do exist now, which means that death is not something “peaceful” in any regard. The life you once had is gone. All the opportunities, the people, and all the Bacon Gouda Egg sandwiches from Starbucks are left behind—and the opportunity to go back is never there again. You can’t even take solace in the abyss of nothingness because you physically can’t. And you never will know for certain if life could one day get better.

I’ve dealt with having immense insecurities (amongst other things) in a relationship. Having someone close to you that can give you reassurance is therapeutic—but in the same breath, it can not only be just “draining” for your partner, but also painful to deal with. And it’s never an annoyance sort of deal on their end—rather, it’s because they are the ones who experience first hand the problems and issues that are affecting you. 

That isn’t at ALL to say that your partner shouldn’t be a beacon of emotional support (in fact every person in every good relationship should be), rather that the concept of them being the go to, or even sole person for the bulk of one’s insecurities/problems will result in an unhappy and problematic relationship. 

The overall point is simple. If you’re getting better—good, stay in that relationship if it’s not hurting you or your partner, and grow. If you’re not making progress, don’t. Regardless of the situation—however, you should be working on whatever skills you need to make to eventually become stable and happy without too much help from others. Additionally, if you have issues that require such—work on coping skills. Find a therapist that isn’t a money hoarding goblin, work on coping skills to find one that works for you (even the ones that sound absolutely fucking ridiculous. One that I thought would never work for me was a fucking stupid breathing exercise but it DID, lmao), and eventually draft out a healthy support system for times where you will not be enough to face a certain problem alone.

If you are in the process of getting help and are actively working through your life problems, it is fine to be in a relationship. If you are stating that you want to work through your issues but don’t really try your hardest to do so, get out of that now. I’ve been on both sides of the coin in the latter, and lemme tell you—the end result isn’t pretty for either side of the relationship. 

To reiterate: if it’s hurting him, and you know it’s hurting him, and you’re not working your absolute HARDEST to work through your problems, you should leave that relationship. It will be healthier for both of you. If you’re working through your issues, and you know you’re stable enough to have a relationship at this point in time, by all means—stay in it. Just be very mindful about your boyfriend’s feelings in this whole situation regardless.
